intro: Kompass Skills plan a project properly, then build it in sequences of work units that run back to back without pausing. Every unit and every sequence ends with a written hand-over saved with the code, so the next agent picks up from the record and never from a session's memory.

lifecycle.what: Brief, module map, architecture, UI mockups you click through, decisions. One approval.
One-page briefs grouped into sequences, each ending at a point you can walk through.
Units built back to back, each in a fresh session with kompass-build.
What was achieved, what is parked, and walkthrough steps for you.
You try it; your words and any problems are recorded. Problems become the next sequence's first units.
Starts from the hand-over and your recorded walkthrough.

kompass-plan.plain: Plans a project or phase with you, before any code is written.
kompass-plan.when: Start of a project or phase; re-planning; reviewing the plan.
reads: The existing code, for a project already under way
The project's design tokens, for mockups
produces: Brief and approval record
Module map: purpose, front door, owned files, rules with their tests
Architecture with diagrams of each key journey
Interactive mockups for each UI decision
Decision records
Sequences: where each walkthrough falls
The planning page
stops: Only for your answers and your one approval
questions: For Layerware, should the module map start from the existing LiteBench architecture document, or be rewritten fresh?
How do you want to review mockups: one decision at a time in chat, or a review session over the whole set?
Should every UI decision get a mockup, or only those with real alternatives?

kompass-units.plain: Turns the approved plan into short work-unit briefs, grouped into sequences.
kompass-units.when: After plan approval; whenever a new unit, defect or follow-up is needed.
reads: The approved plan, module map, decisions and mockups
Walkthrough feedback, for problems to fix first
produces: One-page unit briefs: outcome, criteria with proving tests, owned files, out of scope, dependencies
Sequence files with each sequence's goal and units
stops: Never; new units on an approved plan need no approval unless they change the outcome
questions: What is the right size for a unit: about half a day of agent work?
Should units keep Layerware's WU numbering, continuing from WU-0130?
Should open LiteBench units be carried over, or re-planned?

kompass-build.plain: Builds one unit from start to finish and writes its hand-over.
kompass-build.when: For one unit, usually started by kompass-run.
reads: The latest sequence hand-over and your walkthrough feedback
Hand-overs of the units it depends on and the last two delivered
produces: Failing test first, then the fix in the owning module
Independent review on the pull request
Merged code once CI is green
The unit hand-over: what changed, tests, review findings, decisions, known issues, a note for the next unit, evidence
stops: A cause that cannot be proven
A change to the approved outcome
questions: How many CI attempts on one cause before a unit is parked: three?
Should browser tests run locally for every UI unit, or only for screens the mockup covers?
Should the review verdict be enforced by a CI check, or trusted?

kompass-run.plain: Runs a whole sequence unattended, hands it over for your walkthrough, then records what you found.
kompass-run.when: "Run", "continue", "build the next sequence", "hand over sequence N", "I'm ready to try it", "record the walkthrough".
produces: Units built back to back in fresh sessions
Parked units with written reasons
The sequence hand-over with walkthrough steps
Your walkthrough feedback, recorded with your words
Your copy brought up to date and the app started for the walkthrough, without you thinking about where the code lives
New units for problems you found
stops: At the end of every sequence, for your walkthrough
When the repository's safety settings are missing
questions: How should you hear that a sequence is ready to walk through: a phone notification, an email, or the planning page?
Should two units run at once by default when they share no files?
decided: The runner lives on the Hetzner box, in its own container. Darren: "runner has to sit on hetzner. - that's what we built it for".

kompass-find.plain: Finds what was done, when and why, when something breaks later.
kompass-find.when: Before writing a defect unit; whenever an agent needs project history.
reads: Decision records and the module map
Git history (commits start with the unit id) and pull requests
produces: The unit or units involved, with the hand-over or decision lines that explain them
questions: Is plain text search enough, or do we want an index like LiteBench's search?

kompass-builder.plain: Writes the code for one bounded piece of a unit, test first, inside its owned files.
questions: Should a builder pushed to high effort stay on Sonnet, or should a second failure at high effort move the piece to Opus?
kompass-builder.why: Coding from a precise brief: Sonnet writes good code quickly and costs far less, so it does the bulk of the typing.

kompass-reviewer.plain: Checks a unit's changes independently and approves or asks for changes, on correctness, privacy, evidence and ownership.
questions: Which other kinds of unit, beyond privacy, figures and access, should always get a high-effort review?
kompass-reviewer.why: Adversarial checking: a second Opus, in a fresh context, with no stake in the code it reviews.

kompass-searcher.plain: Answers one bounded search or research question across the code, the Kompass records, git history or the web, and returns pointers with short excerpts.
kompass-searcher.why: Searching and reading at volume: Haiku is fast and cheap, so wide sweeps cost little and keep the coordinator's context clean.
questions: Should it also do outside research (other products, library documentation), or should that stay with Opus?

safety: Main only takes changes through pull requests, with one required CI check.
Each pull request is re-tested on top of the latest main before it merges.
Pull requests merge automatically once green.
CI runs the full tests, the two tripwires (locked files; switched-off tests) and the scanners, whichever tool wrote the code.
The destructive-command guard on your Mac stays as a backstop.

coordinator.name: Coordinator
coordinator.plain: The main session in every skill. It plans, writes units, decides each build's approach, briefs the helpers, judges what they return and writes every hand-over.
coordinator.why: Judgement and adversarial thinking: Opus is strongest at deciding what to build and spotting what is wrong.

effortRule: Every model runs at medium effort by default and is pushed to high effort when the work needs it: when one cause fails twice, when a builder fails twice on the same test, and for reviews of units that touch privacy, figures or access.
